D'ALBERT'S =" WN ABE Piano 


_ **Duting my recent sojourn here, I had frequent opportunities to make myself acquainted with the 
Knabe Pianos, and from fullest. conviction I declare them to be the best instruments of America. 
Should I return here for artistic purposes, which may be the case very soon, I shall most certainly use 
the pianos of this celebrated make. I give this testimonial with pleasure, voluntarily, and. entirely 
tinsolicited by the house of Knahe.” 


New York, May 16th, 1890. | igo EUGEN D'ALBERT. 
Von BULOW'S ze OWN A B = PIANO 
TH E ‘ ’ PRARLIET SEISED 
‘: PEERLESS a bheanaEeeBeS 


“The Knabe Pianos, which I did not know before, having been chosen for my present concert tour 
inthe United. States by my impresario, and accepted by me on the recommendation of my friend, 
Bechstein, acduainted with their merits: Had I known these Pianos as I do now I would have chosen 

ae -by inka as their sound and touch are more sympathetic to my ears and hands than all others 
of the country.” | 


New York, 16th of April, 1889. Sy Signed, DR. HANS von BULOW. 


THIS PAIR OF TESTIMONIALS 


Is the strongest ever given to a piano maker in America. They proclaim. in 
trumpet tones the merit, the quality and excellence of the greatest and best of Ameri- 
can pianos. Comiing, as they do, from the world’s two greatest pianists, these spon- . 
taneous letters are most significant. The letter of D’Albert is the most signal testimony 
to the merit of a piano ever given by a great artist, coming as it did after a long 


concert tour, Wherein he used-exclusively a rival of piano.

GENERAL SECRETARY’S REPORT. 


In a recent issue of the New York Christian Advocate Mr. R. R. McBurney, in an 
article on the Young Men’s Christian Associations, gives the following reasons why 
they succeed : 

“ First.—They meet a real and felt need. Young men will have places of resort 
in which to spend leisure hours. 

Second.—The recognition by the Associations of the subordinate relation they 
sustain to the Church of Christ. 

Third.—The prominence given to the study of the Scriptures, the necessity of the 
new birth, and the work of the Holy Spirit in renewal of heart and life. 

Fourth.—The confining of the work to young men by young men.” 

The future grows brighter and the Association horizon broadens with each year. 
At first it was the aim to reach the young men of a single warehouse, then a town or 
city, then a Province or state, then a country, then a union of adjacent countries, and 
to-day, only 45 years from its inception, and while its ‘‘ founder ” still lives, the field 
has broadened so as to include the YOUNG MEN OF THE WORLD. Let us mention 
three lines of advance which have been made during the past year : 

first.—Buildings represent permament growth and future usefulness. At present 
there are 205 owned by the Associations, valued at $8,352,910. Fifty of these have 
been added during the year, and 96 Associations report lots purchased and buildings 
in progress or in view. ‘This shows the confidence which the churches, through their 
Christian business men, have in the present and future value of this special work. 

Second.—The great needs of the young men of the East have pressed upon the 
hearts of the Christian young men of the West. The adaptability of the Association 
lines of work in these fields is being tested with surprising results. Mr. J. T. Swift is 
now erecting a building in Tokio, Japan, the funds for which were freely subscribed in 
America last summer. Mr. David McConoughy, formerly Secretary at Philadelphia, 
has begun in India, and is filled with hope as to the prospects for that great country. 
In a recent letter he says ‘‘that Secretaries are called for at Bombay, Calcutta and 
Columbo; and ‘‘that God is going to lay a responsibility upon the Young Men’s 
Christian Associations of America, greater than they have yet realized, and He 
hopes they will respond to the opportunity.” Mr. Wishard is now in China preparing 
the way for a man to be placed there. The connection thus formed with the vast 
majority of the young men of the world,—for the great majority are still unevangelized 
and in heathen lands, —will make this one of the most eventful years in the history of 


10 


the work. This Association has awakened to its opportunity somewhat and sent $300 
towards the work in India. The Missionary Committee will present a revised plan for 
assisting in this work of ‘‘ extension,’ and we hope each member will take his share. 

Third.—The consolidation of the work in large cities, now illustrated in New 
York, Philadelphia and Chicago, called the ‘‘ metropolitan plan of organization.” 
Instead of a central building and branches, there is one, two, three, and even eight 
Association centres—all called branches—one central Board of Directors supervising 
the whole. So soon as the new building is occupied, we trust this will be the policy 
of the Board of Directors in reference to this city. 


THE NEW BUILDING. 


The Secretary’s time has necessarily been largely devoted to this work. Many 
difficult questions have arisen, and thus far God has honored the requests of the Com- 
mittee, viz. : ‘‘ That their decisions might be unanimous.’? Work was commenced 
August 17, 1889, and renewed this Spring, April 13. We hope to take possession May 
1, 1891: doubtless holding our 4oth Annual Meeting in the new building. The 
successful completion of this building places increased responsibility upon the Board 
of Directors. The financial obligations are very great. Thus far the response from 
citizens and members has been cheerful and hearty. But much more remains to be 
done. The duty of the hour demands that every member bear his part. We ought 
to have a subscription list which will cover the total cost of the building before May 

1, 1891. This is God’s work. The Association has but one aim in its erection, VizZ., 
the extension of His Kingdom amongst the young men of this city. Remembering 
what the man of God said to Amaziah, King of Israel, when he was concerned about 
the hundred talents : ‘‘ God is able to give thee much more than this,” let us show our 
faith by our present effort. Prompt action now will tell to better purpose than at any 
other time, as this can never be accomplished so easily as before the building is 
dedicated. 

THE PRESENT BUILDING 


has been used to its utmost capacity. Lack of room has compelled us to postpone 
the adding of some useful features. The extra effort required to hold our attendance 
at REGULAR MEETINGS at this point increases each year, and to secure audiences for 
special meetings or lectures is so difficult as to become discouraging. 


THE MEMBERSHIP 


now numbers 1,133, an increase of 68 over last year. Two hundred and fifty new 
names were added. Many are withholding taking out their ticket until the opening 
of the new building. A systematic effort has been made to call upon the associate 
members in order to secure their attendance and interest in the religious meetings. 
Fully one-third of the associate members have been thus personally visited, and 46 of 
our active members have engaged.in.this personal work. The results are so satis- 
factory, both upon the active and associate members, that we expect to give such time 
to its supervision that every associate member will be personally visited during the 
year. Twenty-five (25) of the associate members have requested that their names be 
transferred to the active list, having joined their respective churches. 


11 


The following deaths have occurred amongst our members: 


ALFRED SAVAGE, W. P. YOUNG, THOS. GREEN, 
EDWARD RUSSELL, F. GAZELEY, H. WIDDOWSON. 
From our list of contributors who were not members : 
GEO. ROGERS, T. TANDY, J. FOWLER. 


THE WORKING FORCE 


‘s without doubt the greatest element of strength in the Association. One hundred 
and twenty-seven have served regularly on committees, or taken active work in special 
lines. This has frequently called for self-denial; but the Christian enthusiasm which 
surrounds it is the future hope for this work. ‘This development of active members is 
from many points of view the most important work of the Association. Each member 
trained is so much added strength. A force is thus started which will extend the 
snfluence of the Association indefinitely. Bringing a young man to Christ is a blessed 
work. Enabling him to win a score of other young men to the Saviour is a still more 
blessed. The life of an Association must depend upon the constant influx of fresh 
young blood into the ranks of its workers. This demands that much time be given 
to careful supervision, selection and encouragement. The pressure of other things 
has seemingly made it impossible to devote the requisite time during the past year. 
We see our failure, and frankly confess it. Instead of 127, there should be 300 
young men training in active work, and we call upon the Executive Committee to 
see that this fault is remedied. The ‘‘ Training Class” is now recognized as the 
most important agency in this practical development. Three such classes were held 
weekly with ‘‘ Courses”? running from October to April, and four additional classes 
began a three months course in March,—three held in the building, and one every 
Friday evening at Point St. Charles. This made seven classes weekly, giving at 
least sixty of our members the benefit of this practical training in Bible study and 
methods of Association work. Experience proves a three-month course to be better 
than six months, and we hope to see at least six Training Classes held weekly as a 
permanent feature of the work. The policy for next year ought to be the development 
of men, so as to meet the requirements of the enlarged work. The following results 
are recorded from Training and Bible-Class Work during the year :— 

18 members have taken work as Sunday School teachers. 

2 members have entered as students for the ministry. 

1 member has gone to Georgian Bay District for Presbyterian Church. 

2 members have gone as Assistant Secretaries in Brooklyn, N.Y. 

I member enters McGill next October to take a medical course preparatory to 
going as medical missionary. 

We have to announce that Mr. D. W. Corbett has decided to take the full course 
of two years at Springfield. While this is a present disappointment, as we shall 
greatly miss his services during this very heavy year, we know he will be so much 
better fitted for his future work, and shall expect his return in June, 1891. 

We have also to announce that Mr. T. Duncan Patton, who has been a faithful 
assistant during the past two years, leaves in September to enter for a year’s course 
at Springfield. He will carry with him the best wishes of all the members for his 
future success. ; 


12 


Mr. James Naismith, B.A., of McGill, also expects to go to Spingfield in September 
to enter their physical department and take a year’s course, preparatory to taking a ‘S 
position as physical director of an Association Gymnasium. We can afford to be i 
justly proud of our Montreal contingent, and shall certainly-expect them to lead th @ 
School. | fihg 4 

The Board was fortunate sin securing the services of Mr. W. J. Orr, formerly / 
assistant here, but for’some years Secretary Railroad Association, St. Thomas. In” a 
his coming we secure immediate relief in the office and general work, occasioned by : 
the extra pressure and demands upon the Secretary’s time in canvass for funds and 
attention to building details. At the same time, we expect through his coming to 
open the way for a branch at Point St. Charles in the near future. 

The attendance at the Rooms has included a large number of non-members. 
Through the Employment Bureau 558 applications have been received and situations 
secured for 134. Also through the Reading Room, Boarding House Register, and 
the social and religious features of the work, we have been able to influence a large 
number of this class. _The daily attendance has increased ten per cent., making the 
average 350 per day, ora total of 105,000 visits by young men to the building during | 
the year. This is exclusive of meetings. 


RELIGIOUS WORK. 


Six hundred and eighty-six religious meetings for youths and young men were held 
in the building, with a total attendance of 20,445. City pastors have been written to 
concerning 57 young men, who were either ‘‘ enquirers” at these meetings or desired _ 
to unite with their churches. The pressing and difficult part of the work is the faithful __ 
and successful ‘‘ following up” of individual cases, so as to secure permanent results. 
The warning message comes with solemn responsibility, ‘‘ And as thy servant was 
busy here and there, he was gone.” To assist in meeting this important work, we 
suggest the addition of a Church Committee, whose whole duty will be to follow up 
these cases and see they are safely housed in the fold of some church. Besides the 
regular Bible Classes and Young Men’s Evangelistic Meetings on Saturday Evenings, 
a Thursday Evening Gospel Meeting was held from June to October, specially to 
reach the strangers who pass through the city during the summer months. The 
attendance and results were so encouraging last year that the Committee has arranged 
to continue it this year. , 4 

In addition to the meetings and classes there is the large daily work which makes 
the Association what it is :—a recognized place where young men who are tempted 
and discouraged can find counsel, advice, sympathy and a helping hand at any time 
during the 14 hours of each day. There are no statistics by which we can tabulate 
this, and yet in a large sense it is one of the most important phases of the work, where 
most of the time, and thought, and effort of the Secretaries has to be given, and 
where, in so many cases, the results do not immediately appear. 


. 
as 
~~ s 


EDUCATIONAL. 


In addition to the Evening Classes of last year, there was added the Association — 
Orchestra, which has a membership of 12, and conducted practices each week under — 
the leadership of Mr. H. A. Jackson. This has already been, and will continue to be, 


—_ 


13 


a valuable feature in the Social and Religious Work, The ‘‘ Glee Club,” under Mr. 
Coates’ leadership, did effective work until ‘‘ La Grippe”’ came. Besides the training 
which the young men received, all the work of the Association was materially helped 
by it. 

A Literary Society was also organized, and has laid a good foundation for future 
work. They will hope to begin in September with a well-planned programme for 
next winter. This supplies a want we have felt in the development of members in 
reading, debate and general literary culture. The Library has had 7,379 books 
drawn, which shows an increase of over 600 since last year. 


SOCIAL AND PHYSICAL. 


In neither of these Branches are we as successful as we should be. The Social 
Meetings and Members’ Meetings held each month have been only fairly well attended. 
Notwithstanding the difficulties which we might name, we hope to see better results, 
by giving more time to this important branch. We call attention to the report of the 
Athletic Committee, and trust that some suitable ‘‘ ground’ for summer work will be 
secured at an early date. While it is felt to be a necessity now, it will be a greater 
one so soon as we open the new building. The Committee for next year should 
carefully consider this question. 

In addition to the work in the Building, Meetings have been regularly sustained 
in the General Hospital on Sunday mornings. Members have assisted at the Men’s 
Service in the House of Industry Sunday evenings. A Committee of ten to fifteen 
young men has distributed tracts amongst the sailors in port every Sunday morning 
from eight to nine o’clock, and a fortnight’s special meetings have been carried on in 
the 5th Militia District Camp during its session at St. Johns, Quebec. 

The Association was represented at the following Conventions, and Conferences 
of Secretaries :—Orange, N.J., in May last ; International Convention, Philadelphia, 
Penn. ; Provincial Convention, Brantford, Ont. ; and has also assisted in outside work 
at Burlington, Vt., Brockville, Ont., and Quebec. 


FUNDS FOR THE WORK. 


Very few of the members realize the amount of time and effort expended by the 
Finance Committee. Notwithstanding extra expenses, the total cost has been met, 
individual members guaranteeing $140, so as to close with a balance on the right side. 
The nineteen Committees have done faithful work. They have held 128 Committee 
meetings, with an attendance of 868 workers. 

We have not received any bequests during the past year. A pamphlet has been 
published showing the bequests and gifts which were made last year to the Association 
work on this continent. This has been circulated widely, and we expect to hear further, 
In the meantime we desire to ask all our members who have made their ‘ wills,”—and 
those who have not done so ought to do so without delay, —to remember the Associa- 
tion and its future work. Even if you have to increase the amount later on, do not 
hesitate to put ina small sum now. If we do our duty within the next ten years, this 
city should have four centres well equipped and furnished where this special work for 
young men will be carried on. 


14 @ 


Let us be faithful in doing the present work, use wise means in letting the people i 
know what the work is, and what our needs are, and then expect God to supply 
that which is required to carry on His own work. We shall not, nay, we cannot be — 
disappointed. 


THE FUTURE 


will be just as bright as our personal consecration and earnest co-operation will make 
it. The TRUST is ours; we are the stewards who must render account. ‘‘ Have ‘a 
faith in God” according to the revised version reads, “ Reckon on God being faith- 
ful.” Let this promise inspire every worker with hope and courage. Where there 4 
has been failure and humiliation, let there be confession and renewed consecration, each 
doing his own part faithfully as unto God, and not unto the Association, and His P 
Name shall get the greater honor in the conversion and development of a great num- q 
ber of young men who, instead of trying to force their way into the overcrowded : 
professional and business lines here, will give their lives to God for His use in the 4 
great centres of the East,—India, China, and Japan; for we confidently believe the 
young men of this continent will play no unimportant part in the history of the Orient 
during the next fifty years.

D. A. BUDGE,

THE NEW BUILDING. 


During the year twenty-six meetings of the Committee were held. The following 
important matters received their attention : The receiving of tenders ; the reduction of 
cost of building, and the receiving of tenders a second time ; the letting of the main 
contract, which was finally awarded to Messrs. Dickison and Allen, Syracuse, N.Y., 
and the plumbing to Messrs, Robt. Mitchell and Co., Montreal,$(the heating and 
ventilation contract is not yet placed); the re-consideration of and adopting the 
original” or larger plan of building on December 14th, 1889 ; and the canvass for 
subscriptions, and attending to the collection of the same. 

After careful consideration and full discussion on these important points, the 
decisions of the Committee were unanimous. The Board of Directors also unani- 
mously adopted the report of the Building Committee to accept the original plan. 
For this unanimous action they desire to thank God, as they recognize in it an 
answer to prayer. 

Subscriptions : 114 directors, merchants, and citizens have subscribed $50,380 ; 
534 young men, members and non-members, have subscribed $18,665.16, making a 
total of $69.045.16 subscribed by 648 different persons. Cash paid on these sub- 
scriptions last year, $17,692. 38. 

In addition to this 123 citizens have agreed to contribute, but have not as yet 
named their amounts, and 78 are considering the matter. Over 3,000 letters have 
heen written presenting the case to individuals, and two pamphlets issued, ‘‘ From a 
business man’s point of view,” and ‘‘ The gifts and bequests made in 1889 to the 
Association work in this country,” 2,500 copies of each printed, and now being cir- 
culated. The young men have rendered most valuable help in the canvass by personal 
solicitation, which is still being carried on systematically. All this has required much 
time, thought, and effort, which has been most freely and cheerfully rendered. 

This year will be the important one, and double the work will be required, not 
only by the Building Committee, but by the co-operation of all the members, if we 
are to accomplish the desired results.

EXECUTIVE. 


The Assistant Secretary, Mr. D. W. Corbett, having obtained leave of absence fou 
a year, to attend the Springfield School, in order to render himself more efficient, the _ 
Association was enabled to secure the services of Mr. Percy Leslie, who was elected | 7 
to act as Secretary of Boys’ Department and Librarian. q 

The missionary fund returned by Mr. Beal from Japan, was handed over to the _ 
Committee ‘‘ On work for young men in India,” of which Mr. David McConaughy — 
is the pioneer Secretary in Madras, and we have already received most cheering and — 
encouraging reports of an early and telling development of the work in that vast field, — 
With the view of developing branch work which claims our attention, the service of — 
Mr. W. J. Orr was secured early this year, and as Mr. Orr isa faithful and tried man ~ 
in all Association lines, this addition to our staff is a valuable one. i 

The camp work at St. Johns last summer was, as usual, carefully planned and — 
carried out. Both officers and men bear hearty testimony to the blessings resulting — 
from the Christian interest taken in the Volunteers. a 

Urgent invitations and requests have come to us during the year from Winnipeg, — 
also from New York State Convention, and other points, for our Secretary to go and 
help them, and while the Committee regret that it was impossible for Mr. Budge to 
spare the time this year, they are gratified at this evidence that the services of our — 
Secretary are known and appreciated abroad as well as at home. 1 

The thirty-eighth anniversary was held on the evening of the 21st January, in the 
St. James Methodist Church, which was filled to overflowing ; Major General Howard, _ 
of the United States Army, and the Rev. James Henderson, were the leading speakers, 
The occasion was a memorable one. . 

The Committee find many encouraging features in the faithfulness and efficiency of — 
all the employees, the spiritual life and growth evinced by officers and workers, the 
increased love for, and attention given to the study of the Bible, the good work done 
by members of the Committees, but best of all, because of continued testimony given — 
by young men, that through the Association influence and help they have obtained 
eternal life. This is the end and aim of all our work, —‘‘ The young men for Christ.” 


R. HENRY HOLLAND, 
Chairman. 


17 


LECTURES AND CLASSES. 


The prevailing epidemic has interrupted our winter’s work considerably. Sir 
Wm. Dawson opened the lecture season with a talk upon “‘ The Scientific and the 
Spiritual,” followed by Dr. J. C. Cameron, ‘‘ Functions of Physical Exercise ;” Dr. 
w. Grant Stewart, ‘‘ Practical Hints on Health ;”” Dr. James Stewart, ‘‘ The Brain 
and its Functions ;” Dr. F. W. Campbell, ‘‘ The Seaside and Salt Water Bathing ; ” 
Dr. W. Geo. Beers, * The Teeth and their Care.”

ROOMS AND LIBRARY. 


The attendance at the rooms has been, as usual, very large, and continually 
increasing. The tables have been covered with the choicest papers and magazines, 
and large additions have been made to the well-filled shelves of our library. The 
usefulness of this department of our work may be learned from the following statis- 
tics: Readers, 604; books on the shelves, 3,124; circulation, 7,279. There were 
added during the year 7 volumes to the Reference Library and 178 to the Circulating 
Library, at a cost of $230.57, while a large number of books were re-bound, costing 
$73.24, making a total expense of $303.81. The number of papers and periodicals 
now on the tables is 146, many kindly supplied by the publishers free, the others at a 
cost of $242 87. 

As has been before noticed, the boys’ department is most liberally patronized, and 
the greatest care has been taken to supply only the best books obtainable for this 
important class of our readers. Your Committee are pleased to notice the greatly 
increased circulation of works on Physical Health, Missions, and Helps to the Study 
of the Bible, and to Christian work. 

With larger and better-ventilated rooms, with a position more central and 
accessible at all times, with continued interest and watchfulness on the part of those 
entrusted with the work, the usefulness and power of this department of the Associa- 
tion will be greatly extended. To those who have supplied us with papers and 
periodicals free ; to the Finance Committee for prompt payment of all our bills ; 
and to Messrs. Paton and Leslie, our Librarians, for faithful service, we tender our 
warmest thanks, 

FRED W. KELLEY, 


Chatrman. 


18 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The work for Boys has changed somewhat in method during the past year. Formerly 
the work was carried on by one Committee, now the work has been divided between 
the following Sub-Committees :—Religious Meetings, Invitation, Literary, Outing, 
and Branch. The number of workers serving on these Committees is 30. 

The total attendance during the year at the Friday evening meetings has been 3291, 
or an average of 63. Largest attendance, 107 ; smallest, 27. 

Our aim has not been so much to secure a large attendance as it has been to secure 
definite results and to develop workers for Christ. We feel that the Boys’ Department 
must enter the New Building with a strong working force of Christian Boys who shall 
control the work. ‘Two Bible Training Classes have been of great service in training 
workers. 

Mr. Walter Cushing was appointed to attend the International Convention, 
Philadelphia. He introduced the Enquirer's Record Book. Since October last 17 
Boys have been spoken to personally, and many of these are now bright Christian 
lads. 

The Invitation Committee numbers 15, and has rendered good service under the 
direction of Mr. Ernest Miller. 

The following lines of work are carried on in connection with the meeting :— 
A Branch of the ‘‘ Scripture Union,” with 64 members; a ‘‘Band of Mercy” was 
organized this year with 52 members ; and ‘‘ The Triple Pledge” against the use of 
intoxicating liquor, tobacco and profanity, which has 68 signatures; the ‘‘ Savings 
Bank” has done a flourishing business. Total amount now deposited, $980.12, of 
which $399.66 is this year’s increase. The Bank pays an interest of 4 per cent., besides 
a special Io per cent. which Mr. Geo. Hague has kindly offered as an inducement for 
the Boys, which is much appreciated. 

The Literary Meetings were not a success, the chief cause being our inability to 
secure a room on a suitable night. 

Several Oudings were held during the summer, and in the fall the Boys had a paper 
chase across the mountain. Saturday afternoons were pleasantly and profitably spent 
in this way. The Snow Shoe Club was organized once more, with the veteran boy, 
Geo. C. Wells as president ; very successful tramps were regularly held throughout the 
winter. The Annual Races took place during February and aroused great interest. 
The thanks of the Club are tendered to those who kindly assisted in procuring suitable 
prizes. These were presented at the closing entertainment, April 28th. 

The Branch Committee, under Mr. W. E. Cushing, has done a good work at Cote 
St. Antoine. A fortnightly Gospel Meeting is held at the residence of Mr. D. W. 
Ross, President, the average attendance has been about 25 ; the interest has increased. 
Many Boys have been blessed and are now testifying for Christ. 

New Year's Day Reception was quite a novelty for the Boys, and proved very 
successful. Two other Social Gatherings have been held. The Boys turn out in full 
force on these occasions. 

PERCY C. LESLIE, 
Chairman.

REPORTS OF ASSOCIATION. 


MEMBERSHIP. 


Despite the fact that we have had many difficulties to contend with during the past 
year, we are glad to report an increase in the membership of the Association. 
The present condition of our roll is as follows :— 


SENIOR. ~ACHVGL 0 bcos ceRases deeke Sh 558 
PRCGCAE eh wed i Piceins td Pe 276 
834 
JUNIOR. —-ACtiVe.. ce. ee eens creer eee ceee 29

Totati. ¢cnk wah featieaca Nd dite 's' os Ce wee sae e's £,133 
Reported last year....... Wa Saiies A Lat 1,065 
LRETONSE nos oo es ote i ky ce as eh we BK 68 


The Committee regret that more has not been accomplished, and feel that our 
workers and members frequently neglect opportunities of presenting the advantages 
of our Association before the young men of their acquaintance. We believe that our 
membership should be at least 2,000, and earnestly request the co-operation of all 
members and friends of the Association during the coming year. 


WILLIAM TEES, 


Chatrnan. 


EMPLOYMENT. 


Owing to the commercial depression during 1889-90, this Bureau has not been of 
as much service as in some previous years. Although the majority of situations have 
been for small salaries, a number of good positions have been filled. 

Besides meeting with Christian young men, we have come in contact with Roman 
Catholics, Jews, Swedenborgians, Unitarians, Freethinkers, and others. 

Some business houses kindly apply to us when in need of help. We would be 
glad to have others do the same. We inquire into all cases, and endeavor to deal 
intelligently and impartially with each. Quite a few have accepted invitations to 
attend our meetings, and through them have been led to know Christ as their Saviour.

YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


Another year’s work is done. What is the retrospect ? There have been 52 
meetings held during the year, with an average attendance of 94. A slight increase 
over last year. 

The new features in the work are :— 

I. An orchestra has been formed, which, together with Mr. Meyers, as leader of 
the singing, has greatly improved this part of the service. 

2. A Thursday evening meeting was held each week, from June to October, and 
has proved a blessing to many young men who remained over in the city for a few 
days on their way to other parts of the country. 

3. A card, with the list of subjects and names of the chairmen for each meeting, 
was issued every three months, and found to be very serviceable. 

The spiritual results have been most gratifying ; after nearly every meeting anxious 
enquirers were met, and pointed to the ‘Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins of 
the world.” Their names and addresses were handed in to the Secretary, and Chris- 
tian workers detailed to follow up the work by calling on them, and explaining more 
fully the way of salvation. Beginners in the Christian life have been helped and 
encouraged to testify before men what Christ has done for their souls. | 

On the whole, the year now ended has been one of special blessing to many of 
those engaged in active Christian work, and we have only to consecrate ourselves 
more entirely to it, and be fully persuaded that what God has promised He is able 
also to perform ; and seek for greater results in winning for Christ young men who 


will take up and continue the work that we now do. 
J. M. CAMPBELL, 


Chatrman. 


27 


SUNDAY MORNING BIBLE STUDY. 


At the beginning of the year we lost our leader, Mr. D. W. Corbett having resigned 
to enter the Springfield School for Christian workers. Mr. Corbett, by his efforts and 
many sacrifices, had endeared himself to all connected with the Class, and we felt his. 
loss sadly. At length Mr. T. D. Patton undertook charge of the Class. The attend-. 
ance has been well sustained and the interest increased. 

The Class has more than ever developed into a Conversational Bible Study. The 
lessons have been especially adapted to Beginners in the Christian life. The average 
attendance is 26. 

The Committee is composed of nine members, who have held eight Committee 
meetings ; besides meeting at 9.30 on Sunday Mornings for ten minutes prayer for 
the Class. We have 60 names on our roll, and are making efforts to have, during the 
summer months, a full attendance. 


JOHN W. ROSS, 


Chairman. 


SUNDAY AFTERNOON EVANGELISTIC BIBLE CLASS. 


The average attendance for the year was 90. The largest being 148, on one Sunday 
in June. The smallest was in January, being 60. 

The card registration system adopted during the present year has effectually 
removed the difficulties in the following up of new members. The number of letters. 
written in this connection during the 12 months being 578, and the number of replies 
by attendance at the Class on the following Sundays, or otherwise, being 295, which 
amply demonstrates the utility of the method. 

During the summer special topics were taken up concerning the practical duties of 
the Christian Life. From October to April lessons were taken from the Gospel of St. 
Mark. These proved to be useful helps and of practical benefit to the Class. Two 
lessons were also given upon Social Purity, which must have been beneficial. 

While it is impossible to state how many conversions there have been during the 
year, the Committee are able to report that Enquirers were found at the close of each 
lesson who were glad to speak personally about spiritual life, and many of them 
have been led to make a decision for Christ. The most important feature, however, 
has been the development of the general Christian character of the members who have 
attended with any degree of regularity, and the Committee feel confident that the 
young men are being established in practical Christian living, which will be invaluable 
to them in the ycars to come. 

The usefulness of this Class to the various churches and Sunday-schools is apparent 
from the fact that 18 of its members have gone out as Sunday-school teachers. The 
Special Sub-Committee for the Visitation of Sick Members has done excellent work as 
formerly. 

The Monthly Question Drawer has been continued throughout the year, and has 
wrought to the benefit of the Class. 


28 


The Committee sent its Secretary, Mr. W. J. Wright, as its special delegate to the 
International Convention held at Philadelphia in May last, and it was also represented 
at the Interprovincial Convention held at Brantford in February last by Mr. 
George A. Irving. 

The thanks of the Committee are tendered to Mr. W. T. Walmsley, who so kindly 
acted as organist, and to Mr. W. A. Coates, to whom the Committee are indebted for 
conducting the Monthly Practice in connection with the praise service. 


¥. F. RITCHIE, 
Chairman. 


RECEPTION COMMITTEE. 


During the year there has been an attendance of 381 men on duty in the rooms, 
which averages over one member each evening. Besides this, ushers were furnished 
for the Anniversary Meeting, held on the 30th January last, being assisted on that 
occasion by other members of the Association. In conjunction with the Social Com- 
mittee this Committee took charge of the New Year's Reception. Some members 
also assisted as ushers at the Christian Endeavor, and Sunday-school Conventions. 
Twenty-one young men have been spoken to personally about their salvation. A 
delegate was sent from this Committee to represent it at the Brantford Convention. 

The Committee meeting, which numbered eleven, has had an average attendance 
of 10 members. The rooms are now each evening closed with prayer. 

With reference to the future we believe that this Committee, when we enter the 
New Building, will be one which will require to be well and ably equipped to meet the 
large number of new young men who will come in. Members should therefore fit 
themselves by learning all they possibly can about Association work and methods, and 
should also study to be well rooted and grounded in God’s Word, so that they may be 
always ready to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason for the hope that is 
in them, with meekness and fear. 

: R. L. CHARLTON, 


Chairman. 


SOCIAL WORK. 


Your Committee this year has tried to give a greater prominence to the social work 
than it has had before. With this end in view, we decided, at the beginning of the 
year, to hold two social evenings each month ; on the first Thursday the meeting being 
of a purely social character for all—music, games and refreshments forming the 
programme, while the third Thursday was occupied by a meeting of members to 
discuss various points of interest in Association work. In these meetings some very 
important themes were discussed, and committees were appointed to carry out the 


29 


results of the several discussions. Our New Year’s reception was quite a success. 
The afternoon, from 3 to 5, was devoted to the junior department, and the evening 
to our senior members, an arrangement which we think was appreciated by all. 

Our warmest thanks are tendered to the lady friends of the Association for their 
‘nvaluable assistance, so kindly rendered on the several occasions when called upon, 
also to the ladies of the following churches who helped at our monthly socials, viz.: St. 
Stephen’s, West End Methodist (Y.P.S.C.E.), First Baptist (Y.P.S.C.E.), Erskine, 
Emmanuel and St. Paul's. 

Late last fall we were obliged, owing to the small number of strangers arriving in 
town, to discontinue our tea on Sunday evening. Now that navigation has opened 


again, no doubt this branch of the work will be resumed. 
J. WILSON, 


Chairman. 


LITERARY SOCIETY. 


The Committee appointed last fall to organize a Literary Society, after several 
meetings, and a good deal of correspondence with similar Association societies in other 
cities, held a preliminary meeting on 23rd January, when the objects were explained 
and members enrolled, and a constitution and by-laws adopted. Since then meetings 
have been held as follows :— 

30th January.— Election of officers. Readings by H. Mason and H. Bragg. 

13th February.—Paper by H. B. Ames, ‘‘ How Literature is Illustrated.” 

27th February.— Debate, * Is Monarchy preferable to Republicanism ?” 

13th March.—Readings by J. G. Darling and H. Mason. Paper on “ Ornithology,” 
by G. A. Dunlop. 

27th March.—Debate, “ That it would be beneficial to Canada to have unre- 
stricted reciprocity with the United States.” 

24th April.—Debate, ‘‘ That the influence of the daily Press of the present time is 
more evil than good.” 

Sth May.—Paper by W. T. Castle, ‘‘ The reformation of the Church of Rome 
from within.” Reading by H. Bragg. Paper by H. B. Ames, * The peace of 
Continental Europe.” 

The number of members is 34; the average attendance is 18. 


HERBERT B. AMES, 
Chairman. 


MUSICAL COMMITTEE. 


After having had instrumental music at several of the meetings in October, it was 
decided to try and form an orchestra in connection with the Association, and Mr. 
Henry A. Jackson kindly volunteered his services as conductor. Some eight or ten 
promised to attend the weekly practices, and a room and piano were devoted to them. 
Thus the Y. M. C. A. Orchestra was formed, and is the only amateur one in the city. 


30 


The Directors made a grant, which was expended on instruments, stands, and music, 
Practices have been held regularly every week, and good progress has been made. 
The preliminary drudgery has been overcome, and the orchestra has given its assist- 
ance at some of the social meetings. The Committee recommends an appropriation 
of $100 for instruments, which will provide the balance still wanted. The thanks of 
the Association are due to Mr. Jackson for his services. | 

The Committee provided the musical part of the programme at the New Year’s 


Reception, Anniversary, and several members’ meetings, besides assisting at the 
young men’s meeting. 


F. MEYERS, 
— Chatrman. 


INVITATION. 


The motto of this Committee for the past year has been ‘‘ Occupy till I come.” 
Each member has been seeking to carry out this injunction, by God’s help, in going 
forth with the good seed into the by-ways of our city, and we are thankful to God for 
granting us the privilege of seeing the fulfilment of the promise ‘‘ my word shall not 
return void.” Many have been brought to the meetings through the invitations distri- 
buted, some of whom we rejoice to know have been led to serve Christ. An average 
of nine young men on Saturday nights and four on Sunday afternoons have been 
engaged in the distribution of invitations on the street corners and through the 
principal hotels ; 57,000 invitation cards have been distributed in this way. Also, 
during the course of educational work, several of our active members who were 
students in the various classes were employed in the distribution of invitations to their 
classmates. In this way many opportunities were obtained for personal conversation 
with young men regarding their salvation. 

The Committee, through its delegate fund, was represented by its Chairman at the 
Brantford Convention. We recommend a similar fund for all Committees ; ten cents 
per month from each member will be sufficient, if the fund is continuous. Each 
Committee should send a delegate to Kingston next year. 

Two of our most active members had to resign last fall, owing to their entering 
college to study for the ministry. During the past nine years ten young men have left 
the ranks of the Committee to enter Christian work. 

S. MUIRHEAD, 
Chatriman. 


ATHLETIC. 


The Athletic department of the Association work during th 
confined to the tramps of the “ Excelsior” Snowshoe Club,” 
pleasant, although the weather was not the most favorable 


€ past year has been 
which have been very © 
for indulgence in this f 
recreation, Two ‘ladies’ nights” were held, both of which proved very enjoyable. i 


31 


We are greatly indebted to our President, to Mr. Holland, Mr. Packard, and Mr. 
Yuile, for their kind hospitality extended to us during the winter. When it was 
thought that the Athletic Club House would have to be closed owing to the lack of 
funds, the ‘‘ Excelsior’? subscribed $50 toward the fund for the liquidation of the 
Club House debt. | 

In the fall of last year we had a ‘‘ paper chase,” in which about twenty members 
participated. This was greatly enjoyed, and we hope to repeat it next season. 

The great need of this department is suitable grounds where games, such as 
lacrosse, football, &c., can be indulged in ; without this the Athletic Department will 
be almost entirely limited to the work of the Snowshoe Club, as otherwise we cannot 
hold our members together, the more athletically inclined among them doubtless 
joining other organizations, where the surrounding influences may not be for their 
advancement in the Christian life. Weare, of course, looking forward to the opening 
of our new gymnasium, which will be a great addition to the work, but this, in the 
opinion of your Committee, will render the securing of grounds all the more desirable. 


JOHN J. LOMAX, 


Chairman. 


TRACT DISTRIBUTION AMONG THE SAILORS. 


The Distribution of Tracts and Papers among the Sailors on the different vessels 
in the Harbor commenced the first Thursday in May, and continued throughout the 
summer until late in November ; the distributors meeting each Sunday in the Sailor’s 
Institute, at 7.45 a.m. 

Our field of labor is the same as in previous years, from Windmill Point to 
Hochelaga. ‘The Canal work, done in former years by the young men of St. Stephen’s 
Church, was undertaken by this band of workers. The attendance throughout the 
summer, with few exceptions, has been very good, and more interest has been taken in 
the work. 

WILLIAM LAW, 


Chatrman. 


MISSIONARY. 


At the time of the last Annual Report of this Committee, no organized work for 
the young men of heathen lands was in existence, but since then a work has not only 
been commenced, but, in the short space of a year, has developed into an aggressive 
movement which is surprising to all who love the work of the Young Men’s Christian 
Association. 

The International Committee is seeking, through its Secretaries in these fields, to 


organize the Christian Young Men into Associations with our methods of work, and 
train native General Secretaries. 


32 


Mr. Swift and Mr. McConaughy have been appointed Secretaries of the Interna. _ 
tional Committee, the latter for India, the former for Japan. Two buildings are in zh: 
course of erection in Tokio, Japan, one for local and the other for college work, and _ 
both Secretaries are to be natives. In India the work has only been commenced a 
since the beginning of the present year, and the progress made is truly wonderful, but — 
space here will only allow of its mention. Your Committee, during the past year, jam 
resolved that India would be the field to which we would give our support; since _ 
then, we think, the results fully show the wisdom of this choice. At the Brantford. ‘ 
Convention a suggestion was brought forward, asking delegates to bring this matter — 
before the Associations of the two Provinces, so that each Association should havea 
part in the work for India. This is being presented to them now, and, we hope, will 
have good results. Both Provinces should give at least $1,000 per year. Your . 
Committee desires during the present year to unite the subscriptions towards India, 
the Provincial and International Committee’s work in one fund, dividing it as follows + 
India, 75°/, ; Provincial Work, 15°/,; International Committee, 10°/,. We expect — 
at an early date to issue circulars, presenting the work fully to members, and hope all 
will take some share in this grand work, no matter how small. We would like to 


receive at least $700 during the year 1890-91, and if each one will help it can easily 
be done, and it ought to be done. 


i 


S. MUIRHEAD, 
Chatrman,

APPENDIX. 


HISTORICAL STATEMENT 


OF THE 


Younc Men's Curistian ASSOCIATION 
oF MONTREAL 


(Presented at Laying [Historical Stone, New Building, 
Dominion Square, June 12, 1890 ). 


On November 19, 1851, a meeting was held in the Baptist Church, St. Helen 
Street, to consider the question of organizing a Young Men’s Christian Association. 
Rev. F. H. Marling was Chairman. Result: Representatives were appointed from 
city churches to draft a constitution and report on Nov. 25. Their constitution was 
adopted, and Mr. J. H. Winn, of St. George’s Church, elected first President. The 
Rev. Donald Fraser, of Coté Street Church, was asked to deliver the opening lecture. 

This constituted the first Young Men’s Christian Association on the continent of 
America. 

Since its formation this Association has occupied the following ‘‘ homes” in this 
city :— 

Ist. The Oddfellows’ Hall, St. James Street, one room, 1852-55. 

2nd. On Notre Dame Street (near St. Francois Xavier), one room, 1855-56. 

3rd. St. James Street (near Ottawa Hotel), 1856-58. 

4th. On McGill Street (near J. H. Jones & Co.’s present warehouse), 1858-62. 

5th. On St. James Street (over Bank of Upper Canada), 1862-63. 

6th. On St. James Street (next Post Office), 1863-66. First General Secretary 
employed, Mr. Alfred Sandham, who faithfully carried on the work for ten years. 

7th. Corner Alexander and Craig Streets (present Hope Coffee House), 1866-73. 

Sth. Entered their present building, Victoria Square, 1873-90. 

gth. Expect to remove to Dominion Square, their second building, May 1, 1891. 

From its organization to the date of its entering the present building on Victoria 
Square, the following important points are to be noted :— 

Ist. Their City Mission work largely absorbed the Association. It resulted in the 
Nazareth Street chapel, now controlled by Crescent Street Presbyterian Church. 
During that time three City Missionaries were employed: Rev. Samuel Massey, Rev. 
C. P. Watson and Mr. Jno. Milne. 

2nd. The ‘‘ Out-Door Relief” was organized, the rooms of the Association being 
given to this work one day of each week. This is now done by the House of Industry. 


a 


) 
v 


3rd. * The Seamen’s Mission” was organized, and for many years carried on by the 
Association. Now the Sailors’ Institute. 

4th. ‘*‘ The Soldiers’ Mission,” continued until the Imperial troops were removed. 

5th. The Hospital Mission, still continued. P 

6th. A Mission to the newly-arrived Emigrants. 

With the exception of a weekly meeting for prayer and Bible Study amongst the 
workers, there seems to have been very little, if any, aggressive efforts made to reach 
the young men of the city. This lack was frequently discussed. 

During this period two important Conventions of the Young Men’s Christian 
Associations of America were held here, one in 1856 and the other 1867. - The latter 
was perhaps one of the most important in the history of the American Work, on 
account of the final settlement of the slavery question, so far as the Associations 
were concerned. 

As having an important bearing on Association work at present, the following 
resolution should be noted, which was discussed as far back as 1856 :— 

** That, as vital piety and earnest, practical godliness are intimately connected with 
a healthy physical system, it is very advisable, in the opinion of your committee, that 
Associations should, as far as possible, make arrangements for the physical improve- 
ment and development of their members. Especially is this necessary in the Associa- 
tions of our larger cities, the members of which, generally, are confined during the day 
to sedentary employments, without any opportunity whatever of renewing their relaxed 
and wearied systems by those generous appliances which are open to the young men 
of the world. 

Your committee would also suggest to the Convention that the establishment of 
some means as are here alluded to would doubtless induce many young men, whose 


hearts have not been given to Christ, to join the Associations, and thus they would be _ 


brought under the influence of active members, and led, perhaps, to the prayer meet- 
ing, and finally to the foot of the cross.” | 

On Nov. 17th, 1862, the difficulties had increased to such a degree that a meeting 
was called by the President—Mr. F. E. Grafton—to disband the Association and 
wind up its affairs. The result of this meeting was a new impetus to the work: a 
canvass in the churches for new members, followed and 200 names were added. 

The frequent removal of their rooms and the inability of the Association to do its 
legitimate work for the young men of the city, led to the discussion on the necessity 
of a permanent Building, anda resolution to that effect was passed as far back as 1859. 
In 1869 the Building movement took shape, and largely through the efforts of Mr. T, 
James Claxton, then President, the Building on Victoria Square was erected. The 
Association took possession in 1873. At that time but one weekly meeting for YOUNG 
MEN was held in the Building, with an average attendance of about 25. 

‘In 1875-76, three years after entering the building, the question of debt became 
serious, the sheriff having twice made a demand for unpaid taxes. The mortgage and 
floating debt amounted to about $20,000. A Directors’ meeting was called, when 


Mr. Stapleton Caldecott, then Chairman Finance, since President of Toronto Associa= — es 


tion, made a stirring appeal, proposing that 100 young men of the City be secured to 


subscribe $100 each, making $10,009, and then the merchants be asked for the a 
balance. Mr. J. S. McLachlan generously guaranteed to secure the $10,000 from the 


s> 


Oo 


merchants. The Secretary agreed to undertake the canvass amongst the young men, 
and in six months the amount was secured. In 1877 the debt was paid, and the ‘ 
Association was free to do its legitimate work. 
The Victoria Square Building has developed the following lines of work :— 
Ist. The Boys’ Department, organized 1874. One of the first Associations to 
undertake this branch. 
2nd. The Work clearly defined to be 46y young men and for young men : not general 
city mission work. 
3rd. The Circulating Library to meet the present needs of young men. 
4th. The Evening Educational Classes for commercial and mechanical young men. 
5th. The ‘‘ Committee Organization ” of the younger members, making a division 
of work, rather than all being done by members of the Governing Committee and the 
paid employees. 
6th. The ‘‘ Training Class” idea, which aims at the practical development of the 
‘rank and file” of the membership. 
7th. The value of the Social features of the work. 
8th. The education of the active members that their responsibility is not Zocad, 
or provincial, or continental, but the Association work is for the young men of all lands. 
As an indirect result of working on the above lines, it may be mentioned that already 
35 young men from amongst our members have given their lives wholly to Christian 
work, as Pastors of Churches, Evangelists, Missionaries to foreign lands, or Secretaries 
of Young Men’s Christian Associations. 
In 1885, the Board began to consider the question of removal to a more central 
and larger building “up-town.” The reasons were as follows :— 
Ist. The present building overcrowded. The various departments of the work ~<- 
conflicting for lack of accommodation. 
2nd. Because nine-tenths of the present members reside north, north-east and 
west of the building, making it more difficult each year to secure their attendance 
** downtown ” for evening work. 
3rd. Because there is no provision for Physical Work, which is now a necessity. 
4th. Because there is no suitable provision for the growing demands of Evening 
Educational Class Work, the Junior Department, or the Social or Religious Work. 
Therefore, after careful consideration, the present central site was secured— 
. The joint ownership of the Victoria Square building with the Bible Society was a 
| question which, after two years’ conference, was settled by the Association paying the 
bible Society $12,000 for their interest in it. 
The following gentlemen have occupied the position of President since its 
organization :— 
1851. J. H. Winn. 1860-61. F. E. Grafton. 1880-82. George Hague. 
1852. Edward Taylor. 1862. Thomas Leeming. 1882-84. J. Murray Smith. 
1853-54. George Childs. 1863. T. James Claxton. 1884-86. Dr. F. W. Kelley. 
1855. James Baylis. 1864. J. R. Dougall. 1886-88. RK. Henry Holland. 
1856. T. James Claxton. 1865-66. David Bentley. 1888-90. D. W. Ross. 
1857-58. Geo. S. Brush. 1867-68. Lemuel Cushing. 1890. Abner Kingman. 
1859. Alex. Milloy. 1869-79. T. James Claxton.
